author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: An Instrument Returned
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The guitar came back in a cardboard box.

That was never a good sign.

Greg stood on the steps of Starwake Pier with the box in his hands and an expression that didn't quite know whether to laugh or cry. The instrument belonged to him. He'd lent it to a young musician named Rowan, who had promised to bring it back after the Listening Fair.

Rowan stood nearby, twisting their fingers together.

"I'm really sorry," they said.

Greg opened the box.

The neck was intact, but the bridge had lifted from the body. One string was broken, and a long scratch ran along the lower edge where the finish had been scraped away.

I felt my stomach drop.

"Oh, Greg."

He looked at the instrument for a long time.

Then he put it down.

"What happened?" he asked.

Rowan swallowed.

"The stand tipped when somebody moved a crate. I caught it before it hit the floor, but the case slipped. I thought I could fix the string, and then I saw the bridge."

"Did anyone get hurt?"

"No."

Greg breathed out.

"Okay. That's something."

Rowan looked startled.

"You're not angry?"

"I'm disappointed. It's an old guitar. I wanted it back in one piece."

"I can pay for the repair."

"Let's find out what it needs before we promise anything."

I looked at him. He was upset, and he wasn't hiding it under a joke. That was new enough to make me proud.

We took the guitar to Brasswatch Open Workshop.

Danse was running a training session on careful measuring. Renn had a row of small metal fittings laid out on the bench. When Greg arrived carrying the box, everyone paused.

"Musical instrument," Danse said.

"Broken musical instrument," Greg corrected.

Danse examined the bridge.

"The adhesive has failed."

"Yes, but the wood might still be sound," Greg said.

Danse reached for a tool.

I touched his sleeve.

"Ask first."

He stopped.

"May I examine it?"

Greg nodded.

The first ten minutes went badly.

Danse wanted to measure every piece before deciding on a repair. Greg knew which parts of the guitar had always creaked and which changes would affect its sound. Both were right about something. Both kept interrupting the other.

"If you clamp it there, you'll change the resonance," Greg said.

"If I don't stabilize it, the bridge will lift again."

"I know, but—"

"You haven't let me finish."

"Neither have you."

I raised a hand.

"Would either of you like to hear the other person's sentence?"

They looked at me.

Renn laughed.

"That seems fair."

We tried again.

Greg explained how the instrument sounded before the damage and which imperfections were part of its history. Danse described the structural repair needed to make it safe to restring. Renn took notes and asked whether they could handle the small fittings under supervision.

By afternoon they'd agreed on a plan.

The bridge could be reattached after the old glue was cleaned away. The damaged finish didn't need to be made invisible. The new string would be matched to the rest of the set. Greg would test the instrument before the repair was considered complete.

Rowan arrived after the inspection.

"How much?" they asked.

Danse showed them the estimate.

Rowan looked relieved.

"I can afford that if I pay in two parts."

Greg nodded.

"Then let's do that."

He hesitated.

"Would you still lend me a guitar sometime?"

Greg looked at the box.

"Not this one for a while."

Rowan's face fell.

"But if you're still learning, I can help you find an instrument you can practice on. One that doesn't cost more than your rent."

Rowan smiled.

"Thank you."

I watched Greg carefully. It would have been easy for him to pretend the damage didn't matter because he wanted to be generous. Instead he'd asked for a repair and left room for a relationship that might become different.

Before the repair began, Rowan returned with a small envelope. They had counted out the first payment and wanted to know whether the rest could be paid after their next shift.

Greg looked at Danse. Danse looked at the estimate.

"That is what the agreement says," Danse answered. "We don't alter a signed repayment plan because someone seems anxious."

Rowan relaxed a little. I could see that they'd expected the adults in the room to be angry enough to demand everything at once.

"Can I help with the repair?" they asked.

"Not on this instrument," Greg said gently. "I want the workshop to do it. But you can watch from the marked area, if Danse says it's safe."

Danse set out a clean tray, explained the hot tools and the safe path to the exit. He did not ask Rowan to handle expensive equipment in exchange for the privilege of being there. Renn took the scheduled shop shift; everyone whose time was being used would be paid according to their agreement.

The repair took longer than Greg wanted. He kept hovering in the doorway, then walking away, then returning with a new question he probably knew the answer to already.

I found him by the water pump.

"You can be upset," I said.

"I know. I don't want to yell at the kid."

"Being upset doesn't mean you're going to."

He looked at his hands. "That guitar was with me when I didn't have much else."

I remembered the storage room, the old posters and the letter he had chosen not to destroy. The scratch on a piece of wood wasn't the most painful part of the repair; it was having to trust somebody else with a thing that had once helped him survive.

"Do you need me to stay here?" I asked.

"If you've got time."

"I do. I can sit with you, or I can help Renn sort the inventory. Your choice."

He smiled, half embarrassed. "Could you just sit?"

I sat beside him on the low wall. We watched the workshop door open and close while people came through with their own ordinary problems. He didn't have to turn the mistake into a forgiveness speech. Rowan didn't have to become his protégé to make the repayment acceptable.

When the first test note sounded from inside, Greg stood so quickly I nearly lost my balance.

Danse appeared holding the guitar.

"Not finished," he said. "But the joint is holding."

Greg let out a breath, laughed at himself, then reached for my hand. I squeezed back.

After Rowan left, Danse began cleaning the old glue from the bridge. Greg watched with folded arms.

"You're hovering," Danse said.

"That's my guitar."

"Yes."

"An important guitar."

"I understand."

Greg looked surprised.

Danse set the tool down.

"I once owned equipment that held my whole sense of identity. I know it can be difficult to let someone else repair it."

Greg smiled.

"Yeah. Something like that."

They worked together until evening.

When the bridge had set enough for the next stage, Danse placed the guitar in a safe rack and labeled it with the date. Greg signed the work order and left his contact information for the final test.

Outside, the sky was turning pink.

"How do you feel?" I asked.

Greg looked at the workshop door.

"Still disappointed."

"That's allowed."

"And a little better."

"Also allowed."

He took my hand.

"I used to think if somebody broke something I loved, I had to pretend it was fine or they'd think I didn't love them."

"Now?"

"Now I think I can tell them it hurt without turning them into a villain."

I smiled.

He leaned close and kissed me, warm and familiar. The smell of salt and wood glue clung to his jacket.

"Want to get dinner?" he asked.

"Yes."

"Somewhere with chairs that aren't broken?"

"That seems ambitious."

He laughed.

Two days later, we returned for the sound test. The guitar played clearly, though the repaired bridge made one low note sound slightly warmer than before.

Greg listened.

Then he played the same little melody again.

"Huh."

"Is that bad?" Danse asked.

Greg smiled.

"No. It's different."

He looked at the scratch along the lower edge.

"I think I'll leave that part."

Danse nodded.

"Your decision."

Greg tucked the guitar into its case.

"Thanks."

They shook hands.

For once, neither man seemed to need to prove he had been the most useful person in the room.
